Organisation of Aboriginal Languages K–10

The diagram (Figure 1) is an overview of the Aboriginal Languages K–10 Syllabus. Across a stage of learning all focus areas need to be taught.

Image long description: Diagram displays the 5 focus areas of the syllabus and their content groups. The focus area Interacting has 2 content groups: Exchanging information, ideas and opinions; and Socialising, planning and negotiating. The focus area Responding has 2 content groups: Obtaining information; and Processing and responding to information. The focus area Composing has 3 content groups: Spoken, written and/or multimodal texts; Bilingual and/or multilingual texts; and Systems of language. The focus area The role of language, culture and identity has 2 content groups: Exchanging meaning; and Communication and identity. The focus area Language awareness and building has 2 content groups: Language building; and Language ecologies. A line that circles the focus areas and content groups is labelled, ‘Understanding the nature and role of language, including the relationships between Aboriginal Languages, Countries and Cultures’.

Creating written texts supports learning

The development of the Aboriginal Languages Syllabus follows Recommendation 2: ‘Clarify and strengthen writing content in syllabus documents’ from Teaching Writing: Report of the Thematic Review of Writing (NESA 2018).

Creating written texts facilitates learning as it promotes explicitness, encourages the integration of ideas, supports reflection, fosters personal engagement and aids learners to think about the significance and implication of ideas. Each subject has particular and specific writing demands relevant for communicating within and about the discipline. Writing about content enhances understanding across subjects and stages.

The secondary curriculum includes:

  • systematic development of expectations for creating written texts which align with the English K–10 Syllabus (2022)
  • explicit writing content to support students to become fluent creators of texts and to deepen their understanding of the subject area
  • opportunities to practise the process of creating written texts to develop and communicate knowledge, understanding and ideas
  • a focus on development of word consciousness and precise use of subject-specific terminology.

Creating written texts refers to the act of composing and constructing a text for a particular purpose, audience and context.

Various methods of transcription may be employed, and a student’s preferred communication form(s) should be considered when teaching.

Balance of content

The Languages

The languages to be studied and assessed are the Aboriginal Languages of Australia, with priority given to the Language of Country where the school is located. The term ‘target language’ is used to refer to the Aboriginal Language studied.

In terms of the language ecologies of Australia, the majority of Aboriginal Languages are in revival. These Language Communities may have some fluent speakers among older generations, but generational transmission has been interrupted within the context of post-invasion Language loss. A small number of Aboriginal Languages are considered to be a first language, used as the Language of everyday communication across all generations of a whole Community.

To cater for Torres Strait Islander Language learners, a Torres Strait Islander Language can be studied in consultation and with permissions from the local Aboriginal Community and the appropriate Torres Strait Islander Community. Exposure to learning or awareness of the Language of Country where the school is located is also recommended.

Students should learn to communicate in the target language, including formal and informal language used in daily life, and an awareness of dialectal and/or regional differences. Students may also learn that the target language has corresponding sign and restricted language.

The learners of Aboriginal Languages

Students come to the learning of Languages with diverse linguistic, cultural and personal profiles, including a range of prior language experiences. Students start school as monolingual, bilingual or plurilingual.

Syllabus content is designed to accommodate the range of student entry points and range of learners, some of whom may have significant prior learning, experience or background in the target language and/or other Aboriginal Languages.

In Kindergarten to Year 6, content is developed for 2 broad student groups:

  • students who are studying the target language as Language Revival learners
  • students who are studying the target language as First Language learners.

In Years 7 to 10, content is developed and presented in 3 ways:

  • students who are studying the target language as Language Revival learners
  • students who are studying the target language as First Language learners
  • students undertaking a course based on Life Skills outcomes and content.

Community consultation

The successful introduction and ongoing implementation of the Aboriginal Languages K–10 Syllabus is underpinned by a firm understanding of key principles and protocols associated with Aboriginal Languages and cultures. NSW schools introducing the Aboriginal Languages K–10 Syllabus will ensure success and sustainability by working in partnership with their local Aboriginal Community. The successful delivery of the Aboriginal Languages K–10 Syllabus will be dependent on expertise and guidance from local Aboriginal Knowledge holders, Custodians and stakeholders to support classroom teachers.

The local Aboriginal Community of the school is an important partner and should be the first point of contact regarding the introduction of Aboriginal Languages into school-based teaching and learning programs. They are in the best position to provide advice on local protocols. To support implementation of a successful and sustainable Aboriginal Languages program, the local Aboriginal Community will be able to make recommendations regarding Language speakers, tutors, resources and historical contexts.

The protocols for on-Country and off-Country learning of Aboriginal Languages are fundamental to the ongoing maintenance of Aboriginal social and Cultural practices in NSW. For content that invites comparison between the target language and another NSW Aboriginal Language or an Aboriginal Language from elsewhere in Australia, the Knowledge holders, Custodians and stakeholders of that comparative Language will need to be consulted and will need to support their Language being studied off-Country. The support of the local Aboriginal Community Elders and Knowledge holders will also be required.

The syllabus acknowledges the need for appropriate ongoing consultation on the development and implementation of teaching and learning programs in schools. NESA, through the Aboriginal Languages K–10 Syllabus, supports the aspirations of Aboriginal communities to maintain and revitalise their Languages and cultures.

For delivery of Aboriginal Languages syllabuses, and for any other units of work with a particular or sustained focus on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and Cultures, NSW schools should work in partnership with their local Aboriginal Community to ensure successful and sustainable learning outcomes.

Further advice on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander principles and protocols is available on the NESA website.

overviewSections.heading: Access content points
overviewSections.html:
Access content points have been developed to support students with significant intellectual disability who are working towards Early Stage 1 outcomes. These students may communicate using verbal and/or nonverbal forms.

For each of the Early Stage 1 outcomes, access content points are provided to indicate content that students with significant intellectual disability may access as they work towards the outcomes. Teachers will use the access content points on their own, or in combination with the content for each outcome. 

Decisions regarding curriculum options for students with disability should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

overviewSections.heading: Life Skills outcomes and content
overviewSections.html:
Students with disability can access the syllabus outcomes and content in a range of ways. Decisions regarding curriculum options should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

Some students with intellectual disability may find the Years 7–10 Life Skills outcomes and content the most appropriate option to follow in Stage 4 and/or Stage 5. Before determining whether a student is eligible to undertake a course based on Life Skills outcomes and content, consideration should be given to other ways of assisting the student to engage with the Stage 4 and/or Stage 5 outcomes, or prior stage outcomes if appropriate. This assistance may include a range of adjustments to teaching, learning and assessment activities.

Life Skills outcomes cannot be taught in combination with other outcomes from the same subject. Teachers select specific Life Skills outcomes to teach based on the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of each student. Students are required to demonstrate achievement of one or more Life Skills outcomes.

overviewSections.heading: Protocols for collaborating with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Communities
overviewSections.html:
NESA is committed to working in partnership with Aboriginal Communities and supporting teachers, schools and schooling sectors to improve educational outcomes for young people.

It is important to respect appropriate ways of interacting with Aboriginal Communities and Cultural material when teachers plan, program and implement learning experiences that focus on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities.

Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) protocols need to be followed. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ ICIP protocols include Cultural Knowledges, Cultural Expression and Cultural Property and documentation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ identities and lived experiences. It is important to recognise the diversity and complexity of different Cultural groups in NSW, as protocols may differ between local Aboriginal Communities.

Teachers should work in partnership with Elders, parents, Community members, Cultural Knowledge Holders, or a local, regional or state Aboriginal Education Consultative Group. It is important to respect Elders and the roles of men and women. Local Aboriginal Peoples should be invited to share their Cultural Knowledges with students and staff when engaging with Aboriginal histories and Cultural Practices.

overviewSections.heading: Balance of content
overviewSections.html:
The amount of content associated with a given outcome is not necessarily indicative of the amount of time spent engaging with the respective outcome. Teachers use formative and summative assessment to determine instructional priorities and the time needed for students to demonstrate expected outcomes.

In considering the intended learning, teachers make decisions about the sequence and emphasis to be given to particular groups of content based on the needs and abilities of their students.

rationale:
The study of Aboriginal Languages enables students to communicate in the target language and learn about the vital role that language has in the transmission of Aboriginal cultures.

The study of Aboriginal Languages provides a unique opportunity to learn about and extend respect to Aboriginal Languages and cultures. Students learn about linguistic features and structures of the target language. Students develop conceptual understanding of the target language culture(s) that enable them to make meaning when responding to and composing texts. Students engage with Aboriginal Peoples’ and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ histories and cultures, to become active participants in community life.

Aboriginal Languages and Torres Strait Islander Languages support the identities of Aboriginal Peoples and Torres Strait Islander Peoples. Aboriginal Peoples and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have the right to access their languages (United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Resolution 61/295, adopted 13 September 2007).

The study of Aboriginal Languages enables Aboriginal students to maintain their connections to kin, culture, Country and Community. Aboriginal students are empowered to maintain a sense of identity, and to learn more about their communities. Aboriginal students have the right to learn their own language as future custodians and caretakers of their languages. Non-Aboriginal students are provided with the opportunity to develop knowledge and understanding of Aboriginal Peoples’ languages, cultures and connection to Country, and the impact of colonisation histories.

The Aboriginal Languages K–10 Syllabus advocates the ongoing revitalisation and maintenance of Aboriginal Languages. As an exclusive and integral part of the K–10 curriculum, the maintenance, revitalisation, renewal or reclamation of Aboriginal Languages is of benefit to the sustainability of NSW Aboriginal linguistic and cultural diversity.

The delivery of the Aboriginal Languages K–10 Syllabus promotes a coherent and appropriately rigorous curriculum, which allows for developmental continuity. The study of Aboriginal Languages syllabuses could lead to an increased use of Aboriginal Languages in the home and community, as well as provide a foundation for further vocational and/or higher education pathways.
aim: The study of Aboriginal Languages in K–10 enables students to communicate using an Aboriginal Language. Students reflect on and understand the nature and role of language, including the relationships between Aboriginal Languages, Countries and cultures. Students learn about the importance of maintenance and revival of Aboriginal Languages.

items.examples:
Understanding that the target language is recognised as belonging to a group of people who are the language owners or custodians.

Recognising that Aboriginal Languages have been maintained and passed down through generations.

Reflecting on their own experiences and why learning the target language is important.

items.examples:

outcomes.description: uses modelled target language in simple exchanges

items.text: Exchange greetings with peers, teachers, tutors, Aboriginal Elders or Community members, using the target language, gestures and nonverbal communication if appropriate
items.examples:
Greeting and leave-taking at different times of the day, using formulaic expressions.

Responding to greetings using culturally appropriate gestures.

items.text: Interact with peers, teachers, tutors, Aboriginal Elders or Community members, using target language, gestures and nonverbal communication
items.examples:
Interacting with teachers, tutors, Aboriginal Elders or Community members, using appropriate protocols such as respect terms, behaviour and forms of address.

Responding to simple questions.

items.text: Interact with peers, teachers, tutors, Aboriginal Elders or Community members to share information
items.examples:
Interacting with peers, teachers, tutors, Aboriginal Elders or Community members, including terms of respect and forms of address, using AAC, verbal and/or nonverbal communication as appropriate.

Sharing information about family, friends, community, activities, events or experiences.

Engaging in discussions, responding to others and exchanging ideas on topics such as responsibilities at home, school and in the community.

items.text: Participate in classroom routines and respond to instructions
items.examples:
Participating in classroom routines.

Responding to routine instruction.

Responding to instructions.

Participating and taking turns in games or activities.

items.text: Participate in classroom activities by responding to instructions
items.examples:
Following classroom instructions or helping others.

Participating in games, tasks and activities that involve turn-taking, guessing, matching and choosing objects using formulaic questions and responses.

Grouping and sorting natural objects from Country.

Accompanying Aboriginal Elders to gather materials, such as nuts, twigs, bark, seeds, shells for use in target language activities.

items.text: Participate in shared tasks and activities by responding to instructions
items.examples:
Participating in customary and contemporary games, tasks and activities that involve turn-taking, guessing, matching and choosing objects.

Working collaboratively with peers, teachers and tutors.

Grouping and sorting items into appropriate cultural categories.

Practising personal skills such as active listening behaviours and showing self-discipline and respect for others in interactive group situations.

outcomes.description: responds to simple texts through words, gestures or expression

items.text: Participate in shared listening, viewing or reading of simple texts in the target language
items.examples:
Participating in shared listening, viewing or reading of stories or interactive digital texts using AAC, verbal or nonverbal communication.

Identifying key words/signs or images in stories, songs, performances or dances.

Making predictions about the plot or characters from the title, cover illustrations or other context cues.

Visiting sites on-Country and engaging with stories from Aboriginal Elders or Community members.

items.text: Participate in shared listening, viewing or reading of simple texts
items.examples:
Identifying familiar words or repeated words in a range of texts by matching, sorting, labelling, or miming.

Identifying specific information about Country such as animals, plants, food, artefacts, and recounting using modelled sentences or matching captions or signs to pictures.

Identifying key words in texts such as Welcome to Country or Acknowledgement of Country.

items.text: Participate in shared listening, viewing or reading of simple texts to identify key words and information
items.examples:
Participating in shared listening, viewing or reading of stories using AAC, verbal or nonverbal communication.

Identifying animals, characters, actions, locations in stories, songs, performances and dances.

Making predictions about the plot or characters from the title, cover illustrations or other context cues.

Identifying familiar or repeated words in a spoken, signed or visual text.

items.text: Respond to simple texts through singing, miming, play-acting, drawing, action and/or movement
items.examples:
Responding to and/or performing songs or stories that include repeated phrases, rhythms and nonverbal forms of expression, such as actions, clapping, gestures, facial expressions, mime and dance.

Responding to stories by Aboriginal Elders or Community members.

items.text: Respond to and share information from simple texts, using illustrations and/or gestures to support meaning
items.examples:
Creating or selecting images in response to a spoken, signed or visual text.

Re-enacting or summarising stories using AAC, visuals, puppets, props, actions or gestures and modelled language.

Participating in a shared performance of a familiar text.

Responding to simple questions about characters and events in spoken, signed or visual texts.

items.text: Respond to simple texts through singing, miming, dancing, drawing, action and/or movement
items.examples:
Responding to customary and contemporary stories by sequencing and captioning pictures, drawing events in sequence, or retelling and re-enacting with visuals, props or actions.

Illustrating and describing main characters and key events in stories, songs and performances.

Responding to stories told by Aboriginal Elders or Community members.

Performing songs or stories that include repeated phrases, rhythms and nonverbal forms of expression, such as clapping, gestures, facial expressions and dance.

items.text: Compose shared simple texts in the target language
items.examples:
Creating a shared text based on an event, experience or performance, by illustrating or selecting images and labelling or captioning key elements.

Composing stories using modelled language and repetitive phrases.

Creating multimodal texts using images and captions or signed language with subtitles.

items.text: Compose shared simple texts in the target language using illustrations or actions to support meaning
items.examples:
Composing or performing a repetitive action chant.

Creating captions or visuals to describe characters or objects in an animation, book or video game.

Composing simple sentences by ordering or matching text or signs and images.

Selecting and labelling images to create a digital story of the learning environment.

items.text: Compose shared stories, songs and performances using familiar words and expressions
items.examples:
Re-enacting or retelling simple stories, episodes or interactions with visuals, props, actions or gestures.

Creating own stories by sequencing a series of selected images and adding captions or commentary, by creating a storyboard with labels or creating signed text with subtitles.

Composing a shared digital text based on an event, experience or text.

items.text: Label objects and images in the target language and English
items.examples:
Assigning bilingual labels to the learning environment using images, annotation or language software.

Creating objects using recycled materials and labelling them in the target language and English for display in the classroom.

Collaborating to create a classroom display with bilingual labels and images about a topic of interest.

items.text: Create simple bilingual texts for the classroom environment
items.examples:
Collaborating to create bilingual signage for the learning environment.

Composing bilingual word lists, picture dictionaries, or class reference books of words and their meanings.

Creating bilingual resources for classroom learning activities.

Creating bilingual captions for a photographic display about a class event or experience.

items.text: Create simple bilingual/multilingual texts for the classroom environment
items.examples:
Creating bilingual/multilingual word lists, picture dictionaries or reference books of words and their meanings.

Creating and performing short bilingual/multilingual chants, songs, raps that move between the target language and other known languages.

Creating bilingual/multilingual resources for learning activities.

Creating bilingual/multilingual captions for a photographic display about a class event or experience.

items.text: Recognise the sounds of the target language
items.examples:
Recognising when the target language is being spoken and distinguishing sounds of the language from English sounds and other known languages.

Using imitation and repetition to recognise specific target language sounds that do not exist in English.

Applying sound patterns in song and recognising how words and expressions can be separated into syllables to fit different tunes and rhythms or recognising handshape, position and movement of signs in Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Sign Languages.

Singing, reciting or repeating, focusing on pronunciation, phrasing or intonation.

items.text: Recognise features of the target language sound system, including pitch, accent, rhythm and intonation
items.examples:
Recognising pitch, accent, rhythm or intonation in different texts such as stories, conversations and songs.

Identifying statements, questions and commands based on intonation.

Recognising and producing distinctive target language sounds or producing handshape, position and movement of signs in Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Sign Languages.

items.text: Recognise the different sounds, intonation and rhythms of the target language and how sounds and words relate to the writing system
items.examples:
Recognising the sounds and syllables of familiar spoken words or recognising handshapes, positions or movements of familiar signs.

Understanding how speech sounds join to form syllables, morphemes and complete words and phrases or how to join features of Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Sign Languages to produce complete words or phrases.

Understanding how the writing system represents sounds and meanings, associating individual sounds or a range of sounds with particular letters and combinations of letters.

focusAreas.title: The role of language, culture and identity

outcomes.description: explains the interrelationship between language, culture and identity

items.text: Explain how and why language use varies according to social and cultural contexts, relationships and purposes
items.examples:
Comparing and discussing how values or attitudes are reflected in the target language and another language.

Composing a bilingual script for a performance that encourages audiences to reflect on Aboriginal cultures, significant celebrations or historical events.

Creating bilingual learning resources for younger students of the target language.

items.text: Create a range of bilingual texts and resources to support language learning in the school and wider community
items.examples:
Creating a bilingual script for performances that reflect on Aboriginal culture, significant celebrations or historical events.

Creating captions or commentaries in the target language and in English to accompany texts.

Creating bilingual texts and considering how these shape identity.

Using ICT as appropriate to create a glossary of culture-specific terms or expressions in the target language with explanations in English.

items.text: Create a range of bilingual/multilingual texts and resources for language learning
items.examples:
Composing a bilingual/multilingual text such as a storybook or script that explores a contemporary issue.

Role-playing bilingual/multilingual interpreting in a range of contexts.

Translating literary texts using dictionaries to develop their own linguistic repertoire and an understanding of the risks of word-for-word translation.

Analysing a translated literary text, such as a poem or short story, and comparing with the original text, to show how translators represent the original intention of authors.

items.text: Apply intonation and phrasing patterns of the target language to convey meaning
items.examples:
Applying stress, intonation and body language to convey meaning.

Applying sound patterns.

Using correct pronunciation, intonation, tone and/or pace when communicating in the target language.

Recognising the role of pronunciation, rhythm and pace in creating effects in a spoken text.

items.text: Understand grammatical structures of the target language, and apply them to express complex ideas
items.examples:
Using prefixes or suffixes.

Using expressions of frequency, immediacy and duration.

Understanding that sentences can contain one or more verbs and how they can be joined.

Extending use of negative forms.

items.text: Apply intonation and phrasing patterns in speech to convey meaning
items.examples:
Evaluating how pronunciation, intonation, rhythm and pace assist in making meaning in interactions.

Applying understanding of how tone can convey emotions and meaning.

Understanding that certain sounds in the target language can change or be dropped from pronunciation.

items.text: Understand a range of grammatical structures of the target language and apply these to express complex ideas
items.examples:
Understanding the importance of pronunciation and intonation on the subject word and on the object word and analysing how this affects the meaning of the sentence.

Understanding verb-stem morphology.

Expressing time using temporal expressions.

Understanding attitudinal words, particles and interjections.

items.text: Apply intonation and sound patterns in speech
items.examples:
Recognising and reproducing a range of formulaic phrases and expressions and their appropriate use in a range of contexts.

Evaluating the role of pronunciation, intonation, rhythm and pace for making meaning in interactions.

Understanding that certain sounds in the target language can be adapted or removed in pronunciation.

items.text: Develop and use metalanguage to analyse a range of grammatical structures in the target language and other languages
items.examples:
Making comparisons and connections within and across languages.

Comparing and contrasting the main topical areas of the target language vocabulary with other Aboriginal Languages and/or English.

Discussing relationships between the target language and neighbouring Aboriginal Languages.

Discussing some contrasts between grammatical structures of the target language, other Aboriginal Languages and/or English.

outcomes.description: recognises protocols to maintain and build Aboriginal Languages

items.text: Explore language use and protocols for maintaining and building Aboriginal Languages
items.examples:
Discussing concepts of maintaining, reviving and/or strengthening.

Identifying the owners or custodians of the target language.

Investigating how Aboriginal Languages have been transmitted and recorded across generations.

Understanding that the target language is communally owned and therefore owners or custodians must be consulted regarding its use.

items.text: Investigate ways to maintain and build Aboriginal Languages
items.examples:
Recognising that Aboriginal Languages have been maintained through generations.

Understanding that the target language is recognised as belonging to a group of people who are the language owners or custodians.

Recognising that new words or signs may be formed from within the target language itself, rather than through borrowing words or signs from other languages.

Working with the target language community to create new stories, songs and games.

items.text: Identify available resources and protocols to be followed in maintaining, reviving and strengthening Aboriginal Languages
items.examples:
Exploring resources available for Language revival.

Creating resources to support awareness of the target language.

Exploring that the target language is communally owned and therefore owners or custodians must be consulted regarding its use.

Researching the protocols for receiving, transferring and publishing linguistic resources, including Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP).

items.text: Explore contemporary language use in Aboriginal Languages
items.examples:
Exploring use of Aboriginal Languages in the community.

Exploring their role in maintaining, reviving and/or strengthening Language.

Exploring examples of target language use in the local community.

Researching changes to Aboriginal Languages, including Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Sign Languages, Torres Strait Islander Languages and international Indigenous Languages, that reflect changing trends and emerging needs.

items.text: Investigate contemporary use of Aboriginal Languages
items.examples:
Exploring language-learning experiences with target language speakers.

Recognising ways new words or signs are introduced in Aboriginal Languages or Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Sign Languages.

Investigating language revival efforts in the local community and neighbouring regions.

Creating a multimodal presentation on language revival processes in the target language community or other Aboriginal Languages communities, including Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Sign Languages.

items.text: Investigate and compare changes in Aboriginal Languages and Torres Strait Islander Languages
items.examples:
Recognising English words are borrowed and adapted from Aboriginal Languages.

Discussing loan words that have been incorporated from other languages to describe new concepts.

Exploring how land, water, sea and sky are identified in other Aboriginal Languages.

Recognising that there are many Aboriginal Languages, Torres Strait Islander Languages and Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Sign Languages.

outcomes.description: responds to information and ideas in a range of texts

items.text: Access spoken, written, visual and/or multimodal texts
items.examples:
Engaging with an Aboriginal story in English.

Engaging with shared stories from the target language group.

Responding to familiar stories in the target language.

Exploring target language words or phrases in a range of texts, such as films, radio programs, cartoons or songs.

items.text: Access a range of spoken, written, visual and/or multimodal texts
items.examples:
Recognising key stories of the target language.

Identifying and locating target language words or Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander Sign Languages or gestures by using augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), visual, verbal or nonverbal communication.

Describing main characters and events in stories, songs and performances.

Collecting information about the language words of various regions.

items.text: Access a range of texts to obtain information
items.examples:
Engaging with aspects of culture through signs, gestures, stories, songs, performances or dances.

Creating collective artworks with nature-based materials collected from Country.

Collating information obtained from Country.

items.text: Respond to spoken, written, visual and/or multimodal texts
items.examples:
Engaging in stories communicated by Aboriginal Elders.

Responding to a familiar story.

Responding to the target language by using AAC, visuals, verbal or nonverbal communication.

Connecting their own experiences with a narrative that evokes positive and negative emotions, such as joy, happiness, hope, pride, inspiration, awe, sadness, disappointment, loss or grief.

items.text: Respond to familiar spoken, written, visual and/or multimodal texts
items.examples:
Engaging with a sand story by an Aboriginal Elder, custodian of culture or language rememberer.

Responding to recurring story themes in the target language.

Communicating key elements of a story in the target language.

Making comparisons between stories from Aboriginal Elders and Community members and their own experiences, reflecting on how daily lives have changed.

items.text: Respond to a range of texts
items.examples:
Selecting or creating images in response to a spoken or visual text.

Responding to questions about characters and events in spoken and visual texts.

Sequencing own drawings or selected images to represent a story.

Sequencing and/or organising images and words to describe important characters or significant events from a text.

outcomes.description: uses the target language to interact with others in everyday contexts

items.text: Interact with peers, teachers, tutors, Aboriginal Elders or Community members using verbal and/or nonverbal communication
items.examples:
Using or responding to appropriate greetings in the target language.

Using verbal and nonverbal communication strategies, eg active listening, taking turns and pausing.

Establishing social connections within their school community in the target language.

Exchanging correspondence such as notes, text messages, artworks, invitations, greeting cards.

items.text: Interact with peers, teachers, tutors, Aboriginal Elders or Community members
items.examples:
Introducing or describing themself or familiar people.

Communicating in familiar relationships.

Engaging in conversations using vocabulary related to school or classroom.

Participating, initiating and/or sustaining conversations by asking questions and expanding on responses, or using multiple visuals to expand responses.

items.text: Interact with peers, teachers, tutors, Aboriginal Elders or Community members to share information
items.examples:
Sharing personal information in the target language, using AAC, visuals, verbal or nonverbal communication.

Discussing and sharing their opinion on a topic of interest using the target language.

Sharing areas of Country they have communicated on and with using verbal or nonverbal communication.

Sharing and comparing experiences with others, such as personal perspectives and points of view related to immediate environment and personal world.

items.text: Engage in everyday collaborative activities and participate in classroom routines
items.examples:
Contributing ideas, opinions, feelings or interactions by acknowledging, replying or disagreeing respectfully.

Following instructions in the target language related to transition activities.

Participating, planning and/or organising an activity using expressions related to place, time and numbers.

Participating in language-learning games that focus on specific vocabulary.

items.text: Engage in everyday collaborative activities that involve planning and negotiating, and participate in classroom activities
items.examples:
Collaborating to create displays, multimodal presentations or performances for familiar people or the school community that showcase learning progress.

Planning and/or participating in a cultural experience by preparing and rehearsing language forms, structures or vocabulary.

Taking on roles and responsibilities in the classroom by leading the class in routines using set phrases in the target language.

Participating in individual or collaborative projects or learning experiences that involve brainstorming, negotiating and problem-solving, such as creating multimedia presentations, posters or displays about issues relevant to Country.

items.text: Participate in discussion to socialise, plan and negotiate
items.examples:
Engaging in social interactions with peers, teachers, tutors, Aboriginal Elders or Community members using AAC, visuals, verbal or nonverbal communication about the natural environment.

Planning and negotiating roles for a class event, such as a class display or performance.

Working collaboratively to design promotional materials for a school or community event.

Exchanging information with students and teachers from a buddy school.
